Mapping Sam and Frodo’s Journey

The road goes ever on, and now it keeps the date. I turned Sam and Frodo’s road to Mordor into a lamp where a small light walks the path across the year.

  • ESP32
  • Addressable LEDs (WS2812B)
  • USB-C power
  • Onshape CAD
  • 3D-printed enclosure
  • Cricut-cut cardstock
  • Personal project

Why I made it

I built this for my brother. He and I share a lot of memories from growing up with The Lord of the Rings, and I wanted to make something we could bond over and appreciate together.

Sam and Frodo’s journey is really a story about friendship, about carrying each other through the long, hard parts, and that felt right for the two of us. There’s a lot of soldering in here, but the electronics were never the point. They’re just how I said it.

What it is

It is a framed map of Middle-earth with the route of the Ring’s journey cut out of it and lit from behind. A dim glow marks the whole road, and one brighter point slowly pulses to show where the travellers would be today.

The bright point follows the dates in the books’ appendices. It sets out from the Shire in late September, waits in Rivendell until Christmas, and reaches Mount Doom in late March. Glance at it on any day and you know where the travellers would be. It has no screen, buttons or app.

How the code was made. I’m an electrical engineering student, not a programmer. The firmware was written with Google Gemini, and I directed it, tested it on the hardware, and made it work for my layout through meticulous trial and error. My own work is the design, the electronics, and the physical build, and that’s where this page spends its time.

The experience

I designed it to be ambient. You plug it in once and it tells you something new without asking for attention.

Time as position

On boot it joins Wi-Fi, reads the date from an internet time server, and places the marker. Nobody sets a clock.

Two levels of light

The full route is a faint, steady glow so the story reads at a glance. The marker is brighter and breathes slowly. I wanted to emulate the slow glow of the lettering on the One Ring in the films, so it swells and fades like an ember instead of blinking like an LED.

Even and soft

A single diffusion sheet turns individual LEDs into a continuous line of light, like ink with a lamp behind it.

This uses the same date table as the firmware, stretched across the route. On the real lamp the glow waits in place on rest days, like the long stay in Rivendell, and creeps forward on travel days.

How I built it

1. Trace and cut the route

I traced the journey on the map, brought the trace into Cricut’s design software, and cut the path out of cardstock with my Cricut. The cardstock sets the shape of the lit line and decides where the light can escape.

2. Shape the light

I bent a strip of programmable LEDs to follow the traced path and fixed it in place. The strip has data and power lines that I soldered and wired to the controller.

3. Diffuse it

I took apart an old laptop to salvage a display diffusion sheet. One sheet, spaced the right distance from the strip, spreads each LED’s hot spot into a smooth line so the route looks like one glowing stroke. Finding that spacing took trial and error, and I tested the effect on its own before assembling anything.

4. Power and control

An ESP32 development board runs the lights. A USB-C breakout board takes power from an ordinary charger, so the lamp needs one cable. As for the wiring, as you can see, it is extremely “clean.” (It is not.) It’s a tangle of jumper wires and cable ties, and it taught me the hardware version of a lesson software people already know: the mess you leave for later becomes the troubleshooting you do later. Next time I’ll plan the routing and keep things tidy as I go.

5. Design and print the enclosure

I designed the frame and stand myself in Onshape and 3D-printed them. The back tray has a notch for the controller and the USB-C port, so the board sits flush and the cable exits at the bottom. The frame holds the map and diffuser in front of the LEDs at the right distance for even light.

Parts and specs

ControllerESP32 DevKit V1, Wi-Fi for time lookup
Lights50 WS2812B addressable LEDs on a single data pin
PowerUSB-C breakout board, 5 V from a standard charger
OpticsOne diffusion sheet salvaged from an old laptop display, plus the route cut from cardstock on a Cricut
EnclosureFrame, back tray and stand designed in Onshape and 3D-printed
SoftwareArduino framework with the FastLED and NTPClient libraries. Written with Google Gemini and tested by me.

Takeaways

What worked

The diffusion sheet is what I think makes this project look truly magical. The light spreads through the cutout path like a liquid, and it is exactly what I was going for. I happened to see a YouTube video about different ways to reuse an old laptop, and one method was to use its diffusion sheets.

The soldering and physical construction of the circuit were much smoother than I expected. I spent a lot of time practicing soldering before I attempted the final circuit, and I was nervous about how close together all of the pins were. I did fuse two pins together a couple of times, but I was able to clean up the solder and make stable connections. I secured every solder joint with a glob of hot glue, just to be safe.

What I’d do differently

I would give myself more iteration attempts. I wasn’t happy with the final fit and finish, and 3D printing isn’t my strong suit, so it was definitely the limiting factor for polish. Had I started with low-fidelity prototypes, like cardboard or even paper, I’m sure I would have ended up with a more refined product.

There are also plenty of features I’d love to add in a V2. For one, I’d use a nice wood for the frame to fit the LOTR aesthetic. I’d also add unique interactions during pivotal moments of the journey. For example, the map could flash red when Frodo is stabbed by the cave troll, or turn green as they traverse the bog.

What it meant to me

This was my first taste of a full project, from design to building, to testing, to rebuilding, to finishing. I used to work as an Interaction Designer, where I never got to build anything I worked on. Even a simple project like this made me realize I’d found my passion.

Personal project by an electrical engineering student at Kennesaw State University. Map artwork belongs to its original publisher and is used here for a private, non-commercial build.
